title: Technical deep dive — safe canary rollouts on Redwood Hosted
summary: Northstar evaluated Redwood Hosted canary rollout workflow requirements for safely introducing new model versions/configs. Discussion focused on percentage traffic splitting, deterministic cohorting/stickiness, guardrails (max step size, soak time, approvals), auto-stop/rollback conditions based on SLO metrics, and audit logging/retention/SIEM export. Redwood covered expected GA workflow in Console, underlying routing enforcement, failure modes (streaming/retries), and operational runbooks/alerts. Customer asked for evidence around change control (who approved what), and how rollouts interact with existing fallback policies and multi-region behavior.
topics: Deterministic cohort assignment and stickiness (hashing, retries, streaming)
Guardrail policies: max step, min soak, approval gates, RBAC
Auto-stop/auto-rollback triggers: 5xx, timeouts, p95 latency regression
Metrics comparisons: baseline vs canary cohorts, per route/region
Audit logs: event types, actor identity, diffs, retention, SIEM export
Interaction with fallback routing and multi-region routing behavior
questions: Can we require an approver for moving from 25% to 50% but not for 1% to 5%?
How do you keep a user/session sticky to the canary during streaming and retries?
What happens if a region is degraded—does the split hold per region or globally?
Can we tune auto-rollback thresholds per route and per environment?
Do audit log events include configuration diffs and the before/after traffic schedule?
action_items: Simran Kaur — send Northstar the Hosted canary rollout overview + Console screenshots and current GA target timeline — due 2025-02-13
Ethan Park — confirm policy model for step approvals (per step vs per rollout) and share example policy JSON — due 2025-02-14
Sean Gallagher — share recommended default stop conditions (latency/error/timeout) and how to tune without alert storms — due 2025-02-14
Lena Wu (Northstar) — provide Northstar’s audit log retention requirement and preferred SIEM format (Splunk/Datadog/etc.) — due 2025-02-18
Priya Desai (Northstar) — confirm cohort key preference (end-user id vs conversation id vs request id) and constraints — due 2025-02-18
next_steps: Schedule a 45-min security review focused on audit logs, RBAC, retention, and approvals.
Redwood to provide a draft rollout guardrails policy template for Northstar’s internal change control.
Northstar to identify 1–2 candidate Hosted routes for a beta canary rollout and expected traffic volume/regions.
Follow-up technical session on deterministic cohorting details and how it interacts with fallback and multi-region.
transcript:
Meeting: Technical deep dive — safe canary rollouts on Redwood Hosted
Date: 2025-02-12
Start time: 09:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Simran Kaur (Solutions Architect), Dylan Brooks (Eng, Console & Tooling), Ethan Park (Eng, Control Plane), Sean Gallagher (SRE)
Northstar Support AI: Priya Desai (Platform Eng), Mark Ellison (SRE), Lena Wu (Security/GRC), Jon Alvarez (ML Eng)

----

[00:00] Simran Kaur: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for joining. This is the technical deep dive on safe rollouts on Hosted. I know you all specifically want to understand canaries, the guardrails, and like change control and audit logs.

[00:14] Priya Desai: Yep. We’re trying to move off… right now we do a lot of manual switching between model versions and it’s scary.

[00:20] Simran Kaur: Makes sense. Quick intros and then we’ll go straight into traffic splitting, policy, rollback, and audit.

[00:27] Dylan Brooks: Hey, I’m Dylan. I run Console and the rollout workflow pieces.

[00:31] Ethan Park: Ethan, I’m on the platform control plane and config/policy evaluation side.

[00:35] Sean Gallagher: Sean, SRE. I own SLOs and “don’t page everyone” stuff.

[00:39] Priya Desai: Priya, platform. Mark is SRE. Lena is security. Jon is ML.

[00:45] Jon Alvarez: Hi.

[00:47] Simran Kaur: Great. Before we get into the weeds, can you give a 60-second view of what you’re trying to accomplish? Like what is a “rollout” for you—new model weights, or just config?

[01:00] Priya Desai: For us it’s usually switching from, say, a vLLM hosted thing—sorry, not vLLM, from one model version to another model version. Sometimes we adjust decoding params. And we need to do it without blowing latency. We serve a support agent. So if we go from 1.2 seconds p95 to 3 seconds p95, customer support tickets back up.

[01:20] Mark Ellison: And also we’ve had issues where a canary is fine for 10 minutes and then it degrades when cache warms or whatever, so we need “soak.”

[01:29] Lena Wu: Plus approvals. We need an audit log of who initiated, who approved, and who rolled back.

[01:34] Simran Kaur: Perfect. That maps exactly to what we’re building for Hosted. Today we’ll cover: (1) percent splits, (2) deterministic cohorting / stickiness, (3) guardrails, (4) stop conditions and auto rollback, (5) audit logs and retention.

[01:49] Dylan Brooks: I can start with the workflow from the Console perspective.

[01:53] Simran Kaur: Go for it.

[01:55] Dylan Brooks: So on a Hosted route you’ll have a baseline config—like Model A v1, maybe with certain params—and then a candidate config—Model A v2 or different quant profile, etc. The wizard basically asks you: route, baseline target, canary target, and then a traffic schedule.

[02:15] Dylan Brooks: Common schedule is 1% then 5% then 25% then 50% then 100%. But we don’t force those numbers. The guardrails can cap max step size though.

[02:26] Priya Desai: You said “wizard” — is it a new thing or like… we edit YAML?

[02:31] Dylan Brooks: It’s a Console workflow. There’s also API endpoints for create/advance/pause/rollback. But we’re trying to make the Console experience do the right thing by default and show a timeline.

[02:44] Mark Ellison: We don’t want people to do “click 100%” by accident.

[02:47] Dylan Brooks: Yep. There are confirmations and also policy blocks. Like you can try, but it’ll say “Denied by policy: max step is 25%” or “Requires approval.”

[02:59] Lena Wu: Approval meaning… someone else has to click it?

[03:02] Ethan Park: That’s the idea. Policy engine can require an approver role for specific actions: start rollout, change step, promote to 100%, rollback, etc. You can define it as “two-person rule” for particular transitions.

[03:15] Priya Desai: So can we do like: no approval for 1 to 5, but approval for 25 to 50?

[03:21] Ethan Park: Yes, that’s one of the patterns. The policy can key off target percentage or “step delta.” So it can say: if delta > 20% then approval required.

[03:33] Sean Gallagher: And separately, the system can enforce minimum soak—like you can’t progress until X minutes have passed. That prevents “oops just clicked through everything.”

[03:44] Mark Ellison: Okay, that’s good. Now the big thing for us is cohorting. How do you actually make sure the same end user gets routed consistently? We had issues with like… half a conversation goes to one model and then next request goes to another.

[03:58] Simran Kaur: Yeah. That’s probably the most important operational detail.

[04:02] Ravi Menon (Speaker 1): Sorry, I’m Ravi—

[04:04] Simran Kaur: I don’t think Ravi is on this call. Fireflies sometimes does that.

[04:07] Dylan Brooks: (laughs) It will invent people, yeah.

[04:10] Simran Kaur: Ethan, do you want to walk through the deterministic cohort method at a high level, and Dylan can add UI constraints?

[04:17] Ethan Park: Sure. So the data plane needs a stable “cohort key” per request. We compute a hash over a stable identifier plus rollout id. Then we map the hash into 0-99 and if it’s < canary_percent it routes to canary; else baseline.

[04:37] Ethan Park: The important part is what identifier you choose. For Hosted we support a few: (a) explicit header like “X-Redwood-Cohort-Key” or similar, (b) a field in the request metadata, or (c) fallback to something like api_key + a request id, which is not sticky.

[04:54] Priya Desai: We would pass user id or conversation id. Probably conversation id.

[04:59] Ethan Park: Great. If you pass conversation id, you get stickiness across the life of that conversation.

[05:06] Mark Ellison: What about retries? If the client retries or your gateway retries, do we risk flipping cohorts?

[05:13] Ethan Park: If the cohort key is stable, then no. It will compute the same bucket every time.

[05:18] Jon Alvarez: Streaming? Like tokens streaming back? Is it sticky for the entire stream?

[05:23] Ethan Park: The routing decision is made at request start. The stream stays on that backend. So you shouldn’t see half-stream to baseline and half to canary.

[05:32] Sean Gallagher: The only edge case is if the stream is interrupted and the client restarts with a new conversation id or new cohort key, then you might change. But that’s under your control.

[05:44] Mark Ellison: Okay. And multi-region? We run US-East and EU-West.

[05:49] Simran Kaur: Great question. Mina’s team built it so that enforcement is consistent across regions, but metrics are visible per region. Ethan, can you clarify: is the split applied per region or globally?

[06:02] Ethan Park: The policy is defined per route and applied consistently. The hashing is deterministic regardless of region, assuming the same cohort key. That said, actual realized traffic can drift if a region is failing over and getting fewer requests.

[06:18] Mark Ellison: Right, if EU gets drained, then your global percentages are off.

[06:22] Sean Gallagher: Exactly. We usually talk about it as “percentage of eligible requests” per region. We show “intended split” and “observed split.” Observed is what actually happened.

[06:35] Priya Desai: We got burned by observed split mismatching config on a different provider.

[06:41] Dylan Brooks: In the Console we show both: configured 10%, observed 6% in us-east, 11% in eu-west, etc. And there are warnings if observed deviates beyond tolerance.

[06:54] Lena Wu: Is that logged? Like if it deviates, do we get an event?

[06:58] Sean Gallagher: We can alert on it, but it’s generally a lower-severity signal because it can be impacted by traffic patterns. The higher severity is SLO breach: 5xx, timeouts, p95 regression.

[07:14] Simran Kaur: Let’s talk guardrails and stop conditions.

[07:18] Sean Gallagher: So the GA workflow we’re aiming for includes automatic stop/rollback options. You configure thresholds: e.g. canary 5xx rate must not exceed baseline by more than X, or must not exceed absolute Y%. Latency p95 must not regress by more than, say, 20% for Z minutes.

[07:39] Mark Ellison: We want both relative and absolute.

[07:41] Sean Gallagher: Yep, because if baseline is already bad, relative is weird. Most customers do “absolute ceiling” plus “relative regression.”

[07:50] Jon Alvarez: What about quality? Like hallucination rate.

[07:54] Dylan Brooks: In the initial GA scope it’s more operational SLO gates. Quality gates are optional/manual inputs for now. Like you can pause and require an approval after running your own evals.

[08:08] Priya Desai: That’s fine. We can run our own eval harness.

[08:12] Lena Wu: I need to understand approvals. Is it like you have roles? “Approver” role? How is it enforced?

[08:19] Ethan Park: We have RBAC on the Console and API. We can define a “rollout-approver” permission bundle. Policy engine checks: (1) caller identity, (2) role entitlements, (3) the rollout’s current state, (4) requested action, and (5) guardrails.

[08:39] Ethan Park: If policy denies, the orchestrator returns an error code and message that Console renders. And we emit an audit event for the denied action too—configurable, but generally yes.

[08:52] Lena Wu: Wait, you audit denied attempts?

[08:54] Ethan Park: For sensitive things, yes. At least the “attempted change.” It’s useful for governance.

[09:02] Mark Ellison: That helps.

[09:04] Simran Kaur: Dylan, can you describe the timeline view? Northstar asked about “who changed what, when.”

[09:10] Dylan Brooks: The rollout has an activity timeline: created, started, step advanced to 5%, paused, approval requested, approved by X, auto-paused due to stop condition, rolled back, etc. Each entry shows actor, timestamp, and the diff—like canary_percent changed from 5 to 25.

[09:33] Priya Desai: Is that just UI or is there an API?

[09:36] Dylan Brooks: Both. There’s a “rollout events” endpoint and also these are emitted to the audit log stream.

[09:44] Lena Wu: Audit log stream meaning… we can export to Splunk?

[09:48] Simran Kaur: Yes. We support pushing audit logs to common sinks. If you have a preference—Splunk HEC or something—tell us and we’ll match what we can.

[09:57] Lena Wu: We use Splunk and sometimes Datadog for shorter retention.

[10:02] Sean Gallagher: Internally we retain longer, but what you get depends on plan. But audit events are designed to be exported.

[10:10] Mark Ellison: I’m gonna ask about rollback. Is rollback instant? Like if p95 spikes, does it flip to 0% canary immediately?

[10:18] Sean Gallagher: It can. There’s “auto-pause” and “auto-rollback.” Pause means stop progression and hold current split, rollback means set canary to 0 and route all eligible traffic back to baseline.

[10:33] Mark Ellison: We prefer rollback for severe.

[10:36] Sean Gallagher: Same. You can set severity. Like timeouts > threshold triggers immediate rollback. Latency regression maybe triggers pause first.

[10:47] Priya Desai: How fast do you detect? Because metrics lag.

[10:50] Sean Gallagher: There’s always some lag. We typically evaluate over windows, like 2–5 minute rolling windows. You can trade sensitivity vs false positives. If you do 30 seconds you’ll get flappy.

[11:06] Jon Alvarez: And for token streaming, the request might be long. If you rollback, do active streams terminate?

[11:13] Ethan Park: No, we do not kill in-flight requests when you flip. New requests route to baseline. In-flight streams continue.

[11:22] Mark Ellison: Good.

[11:24] Lena Wu: Do audit logs include who configured the thresholds?

[11:28] Dylan Brooks: Yes. Creating or editing the rollout guardrails is an auditable action.

[11:36] Priya Desai: So what’s the config surface? Is it tied to route config or separate rollout object?

[11:42] Ethan Park: Separate rollout object referencing a route and two targets. The route remains stable; rollout is an overlay policy while active. When you complete, the canary target becomes baseline for the route.

[11:59] Mark Ellison: That’s important: does it actually “promote” and update the route config at the end?

[12:03] Ethan Park: Yes, promotion changes the route’s active target, and that’s also audited.

[12:11] Simran Kaur: Let’s go into interplay with fallback routing. You asked earlier about “existing fallback policies.”

[12:18] Priya Desai: Yeah. We currently have fallback to a cheaper model when you’re out of capacity or if errors happen. During canary, what happens if canary fails? Does it fallback to baseline automatically or to our route fallback?

[12:33] Ethan Park: There’s precedence rules. In general: rollout split decides primary target (baseline/canary). Then existing fallback policies apply within each cohort when that target is unavailable.

[12:48] Ethan Park: But we can also configure “rollback on errors” so the rollout itself stops shifting and routes all to baseline, rather than relying on fallback per request.

[12:59] Mark Ellison: So fallback might mask a canary problem.

[13:02] Sean Gallagher: Exactly. Which is why we encourage separate metrics per cohort, and we can tag fallback events too.

[13:10] Dylan Brooks: In the comparison view you’ll see “fallback rate” in canary vs baseline, if enabled.

[13:18] Jon Alvarez: That’s helpful.

[13:20] Priya Desai: Another question: do you support “minimum request count” before evaluating thresholds? Because at 1% we might not have enough volume.

[13:30] Sean Gallagher: Yes. There’s a min sample size guardrail. For example, don’t evaluate until you have N requests or M tokens, otherwise you get noisy.

[13:41] Mark Ellison: Tokens is better for us.

[13:43] Sean Gallagher: Yep.

[13:45] Lena Wu: Okay, now audit specifics. We need to prove change control to auditors. Do you store actor identity like SSO identity? And include IP? And include “before/after”?

[13:58] Ethan Park: Actor identity includes user id and email (if SSO), org/tenant id, and an auth method. IP can be included depending on the edge layer. For diffs: yes, we store before/after for key fields like percentage, step schedule, stop conditions, target model versions.

[14:18] Lena Wu: Retention?

[14:20] Simran Kaur: That depends on your plan, but for audit logs you can export to keep as long as you need. We can talk about the contractual retention.

[14:30] Lena Wu: We need seven years for certain events.

[14:33] Simran Kaur: Got it. We’ll follow up in the security review and make sure we align.

[14:38] Priya Desai: I want to dig into “policy controls.” Are these per tenant or global? Like can we say only certain routes require approvals?

[14:48] Ethan Park: Policies can be scoped by tenant and can reference route attributes. So you can say: routes labeled “prod-critical” require approvals; other routes don’t.

[15:02] Mark Ellison: Can you label routes in your system?

[15:05] Dylan Brooks: Yes, we have route metadata/tags.

[15:09] Jon Alvarez: What about environment? Staging vs prod.

[15:12] Ethan Park: Same concept. Different tenants or different routes. Most customers do separate tenants for staging.

[15:19] Simran Kaur: Can I ask: are you currently using AWS Bedrock or Azure OpenAI for anything, or is it all self-hosted?

[15:27] Priya Desai: We use Azure OpenAI for some workloads, but for the support agent we’re experimenting with Together and Fireworks because of cost. Bedrock is being evaluated by procurement.

[15:38] Simran Kaur: Understood.

[15:40] Mark Ellison: One pain with Azure is the “deployment” changes aren’t really tracked how we want. Like it’s hard to show an audit trail.

[15:47] Lena Wu: Exactly. And OpenAI doesn’t give you enough knobs.

[15:52] Simran Kaur: That’s consistent. Our view is serving is the control point.

[15:57] Dylan Brooks: If it’s helpful, I can talk through what a rollout looks like end-to-end. Like: create rollout, validate, start at 1%, soak 30 minutes, progress to 5%, etc.

[16:07] Priya Desai: Yes, but also I want to know what “validate” means.

[16:11] Dylan Brooks: Validate checks a few things: baseline and canary targets are compatible with the route (like same request schema), the policy engine allows you to do it, and the schedule obeys guardrails. It also checks you selected a cohort key method.

[16:27] Ethan Park: And we validate that stop conditions aren’t insane. Like can’t set p95 regression threshold to 0% and expect no false positives.

[16:35] Sean Gallagher: (laughs) We’ve seen that.

[16:37] Mark Ellison: Guilty.

[16:40] Dylan Brooks: After validate, you submit. It creates an object and you can start. Starting emits an audit event. Then the data plane sees the active rollout and begins applying split.

[16:56] Priya Desai: How fast does it propagate to the data plane?

[16:59] Ethan Park: Typically seconds. There’s config propagation plus caching. For Hosted we target under a minute. For rollouts we generally expect under ~30 seconds.

[17:12] Mark Ellison: Under a minute is fine.

[17:14] Jon Alvarez: Does it require a deploy on your side?

[17:16] Ethan Park: No. It’s config-driven.

[17:20] Lena Wu: If it’s config-driven, is there a risk it gets stuck halfway? Like “split mismatch” issues.

[17:27] Sean Gallagher: There are failure modes: metrics evaluation timeouts, config propagation delays, or if a region is missing the rollout config. We have runbooks for “stuck rollout” and we have a kill switch.

[17:42] Mark Ellison: Kill switch meaning you disable rollouts entirely?

[17:45] Sean Gallagher: Or disable a specific rollout. But yes, in worst case we can force baseline.

[17:51] Priya Desai: Can customers do that or only Redwood?

[17:54] Dylan Brooks: In the UI you can always hit rollback if you have permission. The global kill switch is typically Redwood-operated for safety, but we can discuss.

[18:05] Lena Wu: That might be okay as long as it’s audited.

[18:08] Dylan Brooks: It is.

[18:10] Simran Kaur: Let’s talk about metrics. What do you need to see to feel safe?

[18:16] Mark Ellison: Latency, error rate, timeouts, and throughput. Specifically p50/p95, and then 429s too.

[18:25] Jon Alvarez: And tokens per second. We care about output tokens speed.

[18:29] Dylan Brooks: The comparison view shows p50/p95, error %, timeout %, and request volume. It can also show tokens/sec, and optionally model-specific things.

[18:41] Sean Gallagher: For stop conditions, we typically use “server errors” (5xx), “timeouts,” and p95 latency. 429s are tricky because they can be policy or quota.

[18:52] Mark Ellison: We want to stop if canary increases 429 because it might indicate capacity issues.

[18:57] Sean Gallagher: Makes sense. We can include it as a signal but we’ll tune it carefully.

[19:04] Priya Desai: Does the canary have separate capacity? Like if we canary to a bigger model, we don’t want it to starve baseline.

[19:12] Simran Kaur: Good question. On Hosted, it’s shared pool generally. Dedicated is different. But the routing layer can enforce per-target rate limits.

[19:23] Ethan Park: We can also define canary max throughput so it can’t exceed, say, 5% even if your hash distribution is off.

[19:33] Mark Ellison: Hash distribution off? Like…

[19:35] Ethan Park: If your cohort key isn’t uniform. For example if you pass “conversation_id” but it’s sequential and small volume, it can clump. Usually hash still spreads but you can get variance at low N.

[19:51] Jon Alvarez: That’s real. We saw 1% become 0% or 4%.

[19:56] Dylan Brooks: That’s why we show observed split and we don’t recommend interpreting 1% at low volume.

[20:03] Simran Kaur: Lena, anything else on audit? Otherwise we can go deeper on approvals.

[20:09] Lena Wu: Approval gates: can it be time-based? Like business hours only.

[20:15] Ethan Park: We don’t have “business hours” as a first-class policy condition yet, but we can do “only allow step changes by role,” and you can operationally enforce the time window.

[20:27] Sean Gallagher: Some customers also do “soak time minimum” which effectively forces time.

[20:33] Mark Ellison: We’d like the system to prevent Friday 5pm deploys.

[20:37] Dylan Brooks: (laughs) A timeless request.

[20:40] Simran Kaur: Noted.

[20:42] Priya Desai: One more: can we pause automatically based on metric breach but require manual approval to continue?

[20:50] Sean Gallagher: Yes, that’s a common configuration. Auto-pause on warning thresholds, auto-rollback on critical thresholds.

[21:00] Ethan Park: And the state machine can require an approval action to resume from paused.

[21:06] Priya Desai: Okay.

[21:08] Jon Alvarez: How do you compare baseline vs canary fairly if the request mix changes? Like if cohorting splits by conversation id, maybe the canary gets more complex chats.

[21:20] Sean Gallagher: That’s a fundamental canary issue. Deterministic hashing helps randomize. But you can still get skew. We recommend using a stable key that’s roughly random across your population.

[21:34] Dylan Brooks: Also, we show confidence indicators / sample size. Not perfect, but helps avoid overreacting.

[21:41] Mark Ellison: Do you support “shadow” traffic? Like send to canary but don’t respond.

[21:46] Simran Kaur: Not in GA scope for this workflow. That’s more like a separate feature.

[21:51] Priya Desai: Fine.

[21:53] Simran Kaur: Let’s do a quick walk-through scenario.

[21:56] Dylan Brooks: Scenario: You have route /support-agent-chat pinned to “model-x 2025-01-15.” You want to move to “model-x 2025-02-05” with a new KV cache setting.

[22:10] Dylan Brooks: You create a canary rollout. Choose cohort key “conversation_id.” Set schedule: 1% for 30 minutes, 5% for 60 minutes, 25% for 2 hours, 50% for 4 hours, then 100%.

[22:28] Dylan Brooks: Guardrails: max step 25%, min soak 30 minutes, approval required for steps >= 50% and for promote to 100%.

[22:41] Dylan Brooks: Stop conditions: rollback if canary 5xx > 1% over 5 minutes; pause if p95 latency regresses > 20% for 10 minutes; rollback if timeouts > 0.5%.

[22:58] Mark Ellison: That’s basically what we want.

[23:01] Dylan Brooks: Then you hit start. You watch the comparison view. If things look good, you advance steps—some steps automatically after soak if configured, others require click and approval.

[23:17] Priya Desai: Does it auto-advance?

[23:19] Dylan Brooks: Optional. We can do manual step progression. GA will support manual and some automation, but we’re cautious.

[23:28] Mark Ellison: We prefer manual.

[23:30] Sean Gallagher: Manual reduces risk.

[23:33] Lena Wu: When you say “approval required,” what’s the UX? Does it notify the approver?

[23:39] Dylan Brooks: There’s an “approval requested” state. Approvers see it in Console. Notifications—we can do email or Slack depending on integration; not guaranteed in first iteration, but we have in-app notifications.

[23:56] Simran Kaur: We can confirm notification capabilities offline.

[24:00] Priya Desai: For us, Slack is best.

[24:02] Dylan Brooks: Noted.

[24:04] Mark Ellison: Okay. Now, edge case: Suppose canary is 25%. Then your system triggers auto-rollback. Does it rollback only to baseline target? Or could it rollback to a fallback model?

[24:17] Ethan Park: Rollback means routing to the baseline target as defined in the rollout. Separate from fallback routing policy.

[24:25] Mark Ellison: And does it mark the rollout as failed?

[24:28] Dylan Brooks: It marks as rolled back, with reason: “auto rollback due to SLO breach.”

[24:35] Sean Gallagher: And we include the metrics that triggered it in the event payload.

[24:41] Lena Wu: That’s important. Auditors like “why.”

[24:44] Priya Desai: Do you have a programmatic way to fetch that reason? We want to postmortem.

[24:50] Dylan Brooks: Yes. Rollout events include reason codes.

[24:55] Jon Alvarez: Another edge case: If the canary target has a different tokenizer or output behavior, can the route be incompatible?

[25:05] Ethan Park: We validate request/response schema compatibility at a high level. But semantics are on you. That’s where your manual evals come in.

[25:14] Simran Kaur: We can talk about structured outputs later, but for rollouts it’s mostly operational.

[25:19] Mark Ellison: Makes sense.

[25:21] Priya Desai: Can we run two rollouts on the same route?

[25:24] Ethan Park: Not simultaneously. One active rollout per route to avoid weird composition.

[25:30] Priya Desai: Okay.

[25:32] Lena Wu: Can we restrict who can even create a rollout? Not just approve.

[25:37] Ethan Park: Yes. Different permissions: create vs start vs approve vs rollback.

[25:43] Simran Kaur: At this point, are there any blockers conceptually? Or do you want to go deeper on the audit schema?

[25:50] Lena Wu: I’d like an example event. Like “rollout_step_changed” fields.

[25:56] Ethan Park: We can send you a sample. It would have: event type, timestamp, tenant, route id, rollout id, actor, action, previous values, new values, and possibly request id.

[26:12] Lena Wu: Great.

[26:14] Mark Ellison: I want to ask about “observed split mismatch.” How do you debug that if it happens?

[26:20] Sean Gallagher: Typically you check: are requests sending the cohort key? Is it consistent? Then check routing logs: we can log cohort bucket, chosen target, and reason. Then compare metrics aggregation tags. Sometimes mismatch is from metrics, not routing.

[26:39] Mark Ellison: We had that. Metrics tag missing and it looked wrong.

[26:42] Sean Gallagher: Exactly.

[26:44] Dylan Brooks: Console also has a diagnostic panel that shows “eligible requests” vs “tagged requests.”

[26:53] Priya Desai: That’s nice.

[26:56] Simran Kaur: We’re about halfway. I want to make sure we cover Northstar’s procurement/security concerns. Lena, besides audit logs, anything else?

[27:05] Lena Wu: SSO/SAML and role-based access, and whether approvals can be limited to a group.

[27:11] Ethan Park: Yes. SSO supported. Approver group maps to RBAC role.

[27:17] Lena Wu: Okay.

[27:19] Priya Desai: On the technical side, are there API endpoints we can integrate into our deployment pipeline? Like “create rollout” from CI.

[27:28] Dylan Brooks: Yes. We have an API-first approach. Console uses the same endpoints. You can create rollout, progress, pause, rollback. We’d recommend still requiring approvals for prod actions.

[27:43] Mark Ellison: So we can do: CI proposes rollout, then human approves?

[27:47] Ethan Park: Exactly.
